name: Technocracy
summary: Technocracy holds that government should be run by experts using scientific, evidence-based and efficiency-minded methods rather than by partisan politics. Legitimacy comes from competence and results rather than from elections or ideology. It pursues a single long-term common good, worked out by reason, instead of bargaining between competing interests. In practice it usually appears as a hybrid, with key functions such as monetary policy and regulation handed to independent expert bodies.
scope: The mainstream doctrine of rule by expertise as it exists today, in hybrid technocratic governance (independent central banks, EU expert institutions, Singapore-style meritocratic administration, technocratic cabinets), as described in Wikipedia's overview and in Caramani's and Bertsou and Caramani's political-science work. Its intellectual lineage runs from Saint-Simon through Veblen's 'soviet of technicians'. It excludes the specific economic program of the 1930s Technocracy Inc. movement (energy certificates replacing money, a continental technate), which is used only as a historical reference point.

furtherReading.title: Technocracy movement (Wikipedia)
furtherReading.note: The 1930s North American movement that popularised the word.

furtherReading.title: The Engineers and the Price System (Thorstein Veblen, 1921)
furtherReading.note: The classic case for handing industry to engineers, ending with the 'soviet of technicians'.

furtherReading.title: Letters from an Inhabitant of Geneva (Saint-Simon, 1803)
furtherReading.note: An early text by the 'father of technocracy' arguing that scientists should lead society.

keyFigures.name: Henri de Saint-Simon
keyFigures.role: Early proponent of rule by scientists and industrial experts

keyFigures.name: Thorstein Veblen
keyFigures.role: Proposed a "soviet of technicians" in The Engineers and the Price System

sources.usedFor: Technocratic attitudes: preference for expertise, anti-politics, dissatisfaction with representative democracy, non-extreme left-right placement

universal-healthcare.rationale: Not a defining issue; inferred from technocrats' deference to public-health expertise and the comprehensive public services of Keynesian-style technocratic states, though neoliberal technocrats prefer market mechanisms.

raise-minimum-wage.rationale: Technocracy has no commitment either way; it would set wages by economic evidence, and expert opinion on large increases is genuinely divided.

markets-allocate-better.rationale: The family is split: Veblen and the 1930s movement rejected the price system outright, while today's neoliberal technocracy manages markets through competition and risk regulation.

public-ownership.rationale: Ownership is treated as secondary to competent management; Keynesian technocrats favoured state enterprise and neoliberal ones privatisation, so adherents split.

tax-the-wealthy.rationale: Tax levels are seen as a technical question for cost-benefit analysis rather than a principle, and technocratic governments have both raised and cut them.

unions-good.rationale: Technocracy rejects brokering between organised interests in favour of one expert-defined common good, and Veblen dismissed trade unions as rival groups fixed on 'the full dinner-pail'.

property-fundamental.rationale: Property is subordinate to efficiency and the common good; Veblen proposed voiding absentee ownership, though modern technocrats rarely go that far.

regulate-corporations.rationale: Technocrats want expert regulators to discipline business, from Veblen's charge that business sabotages output to modern delegation of regulation to expert agencies.

cut-welfare.rationale: Welfare spending would be judged by measured outcomes, not by principle, and technocratic regimes range from generous Keynesian states to lean ones like Singapore.

worker-ownership.rationale: Technocracy gives control to technically trained managers, not to the workforce as a whole; even Veblen's council was of engineers rather than workers.

surveillance-ok.rationale: Inferred from technocracy's risk-management and cost-benefit reasoning, which tends to accept security measures that experts judge effective; critics note its risk of techno-authoritarianism.

legalize-drugs.rationale: Drug policy would follow evidence on harms, and technocrats differ on what that evidence recommends; the ideology takes no stand of its own.

restrict-hate-speech.rationale: Speech regulation is not a technocratic concern, and nothing in its texts settles it; inferred indifference.

strong-leader.rationale: Scholars contrast technocracy, which entrusts authority to experts reasoning about the public good, with populism, which entrusts it to a leader who embodies the people's will; technocracy is also distinguished from authoritarianism.

state-harmful.rationale: Technocracy is a doctrine of expert administration that extends the state's capacity to plan and regulate, the opposite of anarchism.

limit-guns.rationale: Inferred from deference to public-health evidence on firearm harms; technocratic texts do not address guns.

empower-police-military.rationale: Technocracy has no stated position on security spending; it would allocate it by assessed need.

legalize-sex-work.rationale: Not addressed in technocratic thought; would be settled by evidence on harms, on which adherents differ.

decide-locally.rationale: Technocracy favours centralised, uniform expert solutions such as national directorates or continental planning, and critics fault it precisely for ignoring local context.

rehabilitation.rationale: Inferred from evidence-based policy: technocrats would favour whatever lowers reoffending, which research generally ties to rehabilitation.

traditional-family.rationale: Family structure lies outside technocracy's concerns, and its texts do not address it.

same-sex-marriage.rationale: Not addressed by technocratic thought, which has no moral doctrine on marriage.

abortion-legal.rationale: Technocracy offers no moral position on abortion, and its claim to value-neutrality leaves such questions to others.

more-religion-public.rationale: Technocratic thought puts scientific knowledge in place of theology and metaphysics; Saint-Simon wanted scientists to hold the 'spiritual power'.

correct-racial-injustice.rationale: Not part of technocratic doctrine; would be judged by measured outcomes.

gender-social-construct.rationale: Technocracy takes no position on theories of gender.

preserve-national-culture.rationale: Inferred from its orientation to progress: Saint-Simon set the progressive 'progress of the human mind' against the proprietors' 'No innovation!'.

gradual-change.rationale: Modern technocracy works through established institutions such as central banks and expert agencies and values stability, though Veblen and the 1930s movement sought a sweeping overturn.

reduce-immigration.rationale: Technocracy has no stated view on immigration levels, and technocratic governments have managed migration very differently.

empower-international-orgs.rationale: Expert-led supranational bodies such as the EU's institutions and the European Central Bank are standard examples of technocratic governance.

free-trade.rationale: Inferred from deference to mainstream economic expertise; the 1930s movement's self-sufficient continental technate is an exception.

nation-first.rationale: Technocracy aims at a long-term common good worked out by reason, not national self-interest; Saint-Simon described wars as clashes of private interests.

open-borders.rationale: Not addressed by technocratic thought; it has no doctrine on borders.

limit-growth.rationale: Technocracy aims at productive efficiency and abundance; Veblen attacked business for restricting output, though modern technocrats also apply ecological evidence.

drastic-climate-action.rationale: Technocratic governance applies scientific evidence to climate and environmental regulation, and adherents defer to climate science.

tech-solves-problems.rationale: Technocrats trust science and engineering to deliver prosperity; the 1930s movement held that technology had made abundance possible.

expand-nuclear.rationale: Inferred from deference to engineering expertise and the movement's focus on energy; no technocratic text cited here addresses nuclear power.

revolution-justified.rationale: Technocrats opposed communist revolution and modern technocracy works through institutions, though Veblen envisaged an 'overturn' by a general strike of technicians.

experts-over-public.rationale: This is the core of technocracy: legitimacy comes from expertise rather than from popular will.

central-planning.rationale: Adherents split: Veblen and the 1930s movement wanted engineers to plan the whole economy, while most present-day technocrats run central banks and regulators within a market economy.

socialized-markets.rationale: Technocracy cares about who manages, not about worker or public ownership, so it would not make markets conditional on ownership.

tax-inheritance.rationale: Not addressed; it would be treated as a technical fiscal question.

basic-income.rationale: Not part of the mainstream doctrine; the 1930s movement's equal energy certificates resemble one, but modern technocrats are divided.

tariffs-protect-industry.rationale: Inferred from deference to mainstream economic expertise, which generally opposes protection; the 1930s technate's self-sufficiency points the other way.

state-directs-investment.rationale: Technocratic developmental states such as Singapore and post-1978 China, like Veblen's directorate allocating resources among industries, have experts steer investment.

widespread-small-property.rationale: Technocracy values efficiency at scale; Veblen praised chain stores and mail-order houses over wasteful small competitors.

abolish-money-wages.rationale: Technocracy Inc. wanted money replaced by energy certificates, but mainstream technocracy entrusts the management of money to experts rather than abolishing it.

abolish-central-banks.rationale: Independent central banks run by unelected experts are a model technocratic institution.

corporatist-bargaining.rationale: Technocracy seeks one rational common good rather than negotiated settlements between organised groups.

one-party-rule.rationale: Technocracy claims to stand above partisanship and ideology and is analysed as a challenge to party government, though China combines technocrats with one-party rule.

monarchy-legitimate.rationale: Inferred: legitimacy comes from competence, not birth, and Saint-Simon wanted power to follow enlightenment.

democracy-best.rationale: Technocracy grounds legitimacy in expertise and long-term responsibility rather than votes, and people with technocratic attitudes are dissatisfied with representative democracy.

direct-votes.rationale: Putting laws to popular vote is the opposite of entrusting policy to experts, which scholars set against populism's appeal to the people's will.

workers-councils.rationale: Technocracy wants councils of technical experts, not of workers; Veblen's 'soviet' was of technicians and excluded the rank and file.

right-to-secede.rationale: Inferred from its preference for large, integrated planning units such as continental technates and supranational bodies.

natural-rulers.rationale: Technocracy is a form of elitism and meritocracy: those with superior competence should govern, from Plato's philosopher-kings to Saint-Simon's scientists.

political-violence-never.rationale: Technocrats generally reject revolutionary violence and prefer orderly administration; Veblen hoped owners would abdicate without force.

war-builds-character.rationale: Inferred from its idea of a rational common good; Saint-Simon saw wars as clashes of private interests.

separate-church-state.rationale: Technocracy is secular and scientistic, grounding policy in evidence rather than religion.

laws-from-scripture.rationale: Technocracy derives policy from scientific method and evidence, which rules out scripture as a basis for law.

private-courts-defense.rationale: Inferred: technocracy enlarges public expert administration rather than privatising core state functions.

ethnic-nation.rationale: Inferred: legitimacy rests on competence and a rational common good, not ethnicity; the movement called itself anti-fascist.

class-struggle-history.rationale: Technocrats opposed communist revolution and see history in terms of science and technical progress rather than class struggle.

equal-outcomes.rationale: Not addressed by mainstream technocracy; the 1930s movement's equal energy allotments are an exception, and modern technocrats differ.

civilizational-union.rationale: Inferred: technocracy organises around functional and technical units, not religion or civilisation.

self-interest-moral.rationale: Technocracy puts a long-term common good above private interest, and Veblen condemned profit-seeking for sabotaging production.

duties-before-rights.rationale: Inferred from its anti-pluralist focus on a single common good, which ranks the collective interest above individual claims.

nature-intrinsic-value.rationale: Inferred from its instrumental rationality and cost-benefit methods, which value nature for its use to people.

industrial-civilization-disaster.rationale: Technocracy is the governing doctrine of industrial modernity and sees industry, managed rationally, as the source of abundance.

accelerate-technology.rationale: Inferred from its faith in technical progress; modern technocracy also values institutional stability, which tempers this.

human-enhancement.rationale: Inferred from its trust in science and technology; not addressed in technocratic texts.

algorithmic-government.rationale: Algorithmic governance ('algocracy') is discussed as an extension of technocratic, data-driven decision-making, though most adherents keep humans in charge.

restore-past-order.rationale: Technocracy is oriented to progress; Saint-Simon cast innovation and the 'progress of the human mind' against those who resist it.

results-over-ideology.rationale: Judging policy by measured results and evidence rather than ideology is technocracy's defining claim.

direct-action.rationale: Technocracy works through institutions and expert bodies, and the 1930s movement shunned both elections and agitation; inferred.

means-match-ends.rationale: Inferred from technocracy's instrumental rationality and its judging of policy by results.

return-to-foraging.rationale: Technocracy sees rationally managed industry as the source of abundance.

abolish-division-of-labor.rationale: Rule by specialists rests on the division of labor and expertise.

distribute-by-need.rationale: Mainstream technocracy accepts distribution through wages and markets; the 1930s movement's equal energy certificates are an exception.

production-for-use.rationale: Adherents split: Veblen and the 1930s movement attacked production for profit, while today's technocrats manage market economies.

profit-exploitation.rationale: Veblen charged absentee owners with sabotaging production, not with exploiting labor, and modern technocrats accept profit.

dictatorship-of-proletariat.rationale: Technocrats opposed communist revolution and want rule by experts, not by a class.

capitalism-causes-war.rationale: Inferred from deference to mainstream economics and from Saint-Simon's view of industrial society as peaceful.

taxation-theft.rationale: Technocracy extends the state's capacity to plan and regulate and treats taxation as a technical tool.

harm-principle.rationale: Inferred from technocrats' willingness to regulate self-regarding risks when evidence shows harm, as in public-health policy.

exit-over-voice.rationale: Not addressed; technocracy distrusts electoral voice but has no theory of exit.

state-as-business.rationale: Adherents split: neoliberal technocrats apply business management to the state, while Veblen and the 1930s movement rejected the price system.

hereditarian-race.rationale: Inferred from deference to mainstream scientific consensus, which attributes group differences mainly to environment.

organic-representation.rationale: Technocracy wants representation by experts reasoning about the common good, not by organized groups.

total-state.rationale: Technocracy extends expert management over the economy and regulation but does not claim to direct culture or all of life.

national-rebirth.rationale: Inferred from its orientation to progress rather than nationalist renewal.

territorial-expansion.rationale: Inferred from its rational common-good outlook; the 1930s continental technate is an exception.

personal-loyalty-rule.rationale: Authority rests on competence and impersonal expertise, the opposite of personal loyalty.

bound-labor.rationale: Inferred from its meritocratic, efficiency-minded outlook.

universal-morality.rationale: Technocracy claims value-neutrality and takes no moral doctrine.

single-common-good.rationale: Anti-pluralism, the pursuit of one rationally identified general interest instead of mediating between groups, is a defining feature of technocracy.

revive-national-language.rationale: Inferred from its efficiency-minded preference for practical solutions over symbolic national projects.

workplace-democracy.rationale: Technocracy gives authority to experts rather than to votes, and treats broad participation in running institutions as less reliable than competence.

school-vouchers.rationale: Treated as an empirical question for evidence on outcomes; neoliberal technocrats favor choice mechanisms while Keynesian-style ones favor public provision.

avoid-deficit-stimulus.rationale: The family is split between Keynesian technocrats who accept stimulus and neoliberal or central-bank technocrats who favor fiscal rules; the stance is judged by expert analysis.

economic-freedom.rationale: Inferred: technocrats prize expert-run efficiency over liberty as such, and the tradition spans Veblen's centrally planned economy and neoliberal expert regimes, so adherents split on whether freedom needs free markets.

rule-by-example.rationale: Not addressed directly; inferred from technocracy's reliance on expert-designed rules, institutions and measurable results rather than the personal virtue of leaders.

national-self-determination.rationale: Not addressed; inferred from legitimacy resting on competence rather than nationhood, and from technocrats' comfort with supranational expert bodies such as the EU and ECB.

force-without-un.rationale: Inferred from technocracy's preference for rule-bound, expert-run institutions, which suggests deference to the UN system over unilateral military judgment; the sources do not address it.

reason-over-faith.rationale: Technocracy grounds government in scientific, evidence-based expertise and a single common good worked out by reason rather than by passion or partisan will, though 'only' overstates how it treats values and democratic input.

welfare-for-citizens.rationale: Technocracy has no doctrine on who qualifies for benefits; experts would judge eligibility by measured outcomes, and technocratic states differ widely on it.

positive-liberty.rationale: Technocracy is about who governs, not a theory of freedom; adherents range from Keynesian to neoliberal.

work-for-welfare.rationale: Welfare design is left to expert judgment and technocrats of different kinds differ on conditionality.

class-collaboration.rationale: Technocracy pursues a single common good and treats partisan and class bargaining as inefficient; inferred.

sacrifice-heritage.rationale: Technocrats value progress and efficiency but are not defined by hostility to heritage, and the radical Technocracy Inc. agenda is excluded; inferred.

dominated-front.rationale: Technocracy is not defined by geopolitics, and its main forms (central banks, EU bodies) are embedded in Western institutions; inferred.

workers-nation.rationale: Technocracy favors expert administration over class organization of any kind; inferred.

distinct-gender-roles.rationale: Rule by competence and merit runs against assigning public roles by sex; inferred.

ban-interest.rationale: Independent central banks and expert economic management take credit and interest for granted; inferred.

racial-segregation-law.rationale: Legitimacy from competence is at odds with ascriptive racial classification; inferred.

state-class-instrument.rationale: Technocracy claims the state can be neutral and run by experts, though Veblen saw business interests steering industry; inferred.

expand-fossil-fuels.rationale: Inferred from technocratic deference to climate science and environmental expertise, which favors phasing out fossil fuels.

assimilate-immigrants.rationale: Technocracy is indifferent to cultural questions; it would decide integration by evidence, and technocrats are split.

elite-replacement.rationale: Technocrats rest on evidence and expert analysis, and a conspiracy theory of elite replacement conflicts with that.

proportional-representation.rationale: Technocracy has no commitment on electoral systems; it would choose the design experts consider efficient, and experts are split.

national-mission.rationale: Technocracy holds that policy follows reason and evidence, not a national calling.

patriarchy-structural.rationale: Technocracy is silent on this; its experts would follow the evidence, and views among them vary.

political-elite-corrupt.rationale: Technocrats say that the political class is partisan, but they argue it is incompetent and short-term rather than corrupt, and trust experts instead.

heritable-defect-limits.rationale: Early technocrats' eugenics ties are mixed in the sources; modern technocracy has no stated position, so this is inferred from its scientific outlook.

security-forces-accountable.rationale: Technocracy does not address this; expert bodies would favor accountability in general, but it is not part of the doctrine.

night-watchman-state.rationale: Technocracy gives the state broad managerial functions, from regulation to planning, and rejects a minimal state.

discourage-race-mixing.rationale: Rule by evidence-based expertise has no place for racial discouragement, which lacks scientific support; inferred.

equal-moral-worth.rationale: Inferred from its universalist, evidence-based approach to the common good; not a defining position.

socialism-one-country.rationale: Technocracy Inc. opposed communist revolution and partisan politics; inferred disagreement.

settler-state-colonial.rationale: Not addressed by technocracy; adherents would not agree on this.

uniform-civil-code.rationale: Uniform rules applied by expert administration are inferred to be preferred over group-specific law.

restrict-conversion.rationale: Inferred from a secular, evidence-based outlook; not addressed directly.

ban-cattle-slaughter.rationale: Inferred from evidence-based policy over religious norms; not addressed directly.

no-religion-state-schools.rationale: Inferred from technocracy's secular, science-led approach to public institutions.

state-strengthens-encirclement.rationale: Veblen's soviet of technicians and the Technocracy movement addressed no wider geopolitics of socialist states.

consent-of-governed.rationale: Legitimacy comes from competence and results rather than elections or consent, and technocracy is anti-pluralist.

no-neutral-knowledge.rationale: Technocracy rests on the claim that expertise is a neutral, evidence-based guide to government, so adherents reject the idea that knowledge simply reflects power.

trade-surplus.rationale: Not a defining issue; inferred from reliance on mainstream economic expertise, which treats the trade balance as an outcome rather than a goal.

population-transfer.rationale: Not addressed; inferred from the modern hybrid technocracy of liberal-democratic institutions, where expert administration works by rules and evidence rather than expulsion.

initiating-force-wrong.rationale: Technocratic legitimacy rests on results and efficiency, so adherents judge force by outcomes rather than by an absolute rule; inferred, not stated.

competition-drives-progress.rationale: Technocrats pursue a single common good worked out by reason and planned cooperation (Saint-Simon, Veblen) rather than rivalry; neoliberal variants favour competition, so this is inferred.

ban-extremist-parties.rationale: Anti-partisan and order-minded, technocrats would accept removing parties that threaten the expert-run order; inferred, as the issue is not stated.

freedom-as-non-domination.rationale: Freedom is not a central concern of technocracy, and unaccountable expert power sits uneasily with non-domination while efficiency-first rule does not address it; inferred and split.

separated-powers.rationale: Independent expert bodies divide power from elected politicians, but technocrats distrust partisan checks and bargaining; adherents are split.

vanguard-party.rationale: Technocrats want rule by experts, not by a revolutionary party, and the 1930s Technocracy movement explicitly opposed communist revolution and partisan politics.

priority-to-poor.rationale: Technocracy has no commitment either way; it would set priorities by evidence of need and efficiency, and experts differ on prioritising the poorest.

right-to-buy-council-homes.rationale: Technocracy has no stake in housing tenure; it would decide on evidence, and experts are divided on the effects of selling off social housing.

restrict-strikes-picketing.rationale: Technocrats would regulate industrial action on evidence of economic cost, but the doctrine does not commit to restricting or protecting strikes.

population-causes-poverty.rationale: Technocrats defer to demographic and economic research, which does not support population growth as the main cause of poverty, but the doctrine itself takes no stand.

diversity-weakens-cohesion.rationale: Technocracy claims value-neutral, evidence-based rule, and social-science evidence on diversity and cohesion is mixed; inferred from that stance, it would not accept the claim as stated.

offices-by-lottery.rationale: Technocracy rests legitimacy on competence, and Wikipedia and Caramani describe it as set against selection by popular will; random selection of laypeople contradicts rule by experts. Inferred from that principle.

emergency-suspend-protections.rationale: Independent expert bodies and the rule of law are part of hybrid technocratic governance, so suspending legal protections is disfavoured, though technocrats accept emergency powers exercised by experts. Inferred.

price-controls-essentials.rationale: Economists and technocrats in the neoliberal and Keynesian variants generally distrust price ceilings as causing shortages, though emergency controls have been used. Inferred from the evidence-based stance.

party-controls-media.rationale: Technocracy prizes claimed neutrality and independent expert institutions, not party-run information; but Singapore and China-style variants do control media, so adherents differ. Inferred.

party-commands-army.rationale: Technocracy places power in expert state institutions rather than parties and opposes partisan politics, so party command of the army conflicts with it. Inferred.

long-naturalization-wait.rationale: Citizenship timing is a matter technocrats would set by integration evidence; the doctrine takes no position.

representatives-worker-pay.rationale: Technocrats value competent officials and pay arrangements that attract expertise, which cuts against a wage cap; the sources do not address pay directly.

party-discipline-binding.rationale: Technocracy is critical of party government and partisan bargaining, but it also dislikes members voting by self-interest; inferred from its anti-partisan stance.

pool-sovereignty.rationale: Technocratic governance is often hybrid and supranational, notably EU expert institutions and independent bodies handling cross-border problems.

head-commands-forces.rationale: Technocracy gives power to expert bodies, not to a head of state; Caramani contrasts it with populist leader rule.

church-by-bishops.rationale: Church governance is outside the ideology and the sources do not address it.

clerical-rule.rationale: Legitimacy comes from scientific competence, so religious scholars holding final authority contradicts the core claim.

defeat-own-government-war.rationale: Saint-Simon viewed war as a clash of private interests, but technocrats are not class-war internationalists; inferred.

censor-art-for-virtue.rationale: Technocrats are not concerned with moral censorship and favor open scientific inquiry; inferred from the Saint-Simon emphasis on progress.

unlimited-reelection.rationale: Term limits are not a technocratic question; expert bodies tend to value continuity but not personal executive tenure.

recall-officials.rationale: Technocrats prefer judgments by competence and results over popular removal of officials; inferred from their distrust of electoral pressure.

end-foreign-alliances.rationale: Not addressed directly; inferred from the preference for stable, expert-managed institutions and cooperative international bodies such as the EU and central banks.

abolish-rental-housing.rationale: Inferred from the emphasis on efficient, evidence-based policy; housing economists generally favor functioning rental markets, and nothing in the ideology backs forced ownership.

people-in-arms.rationale: Inferred from the central place of professional expertise and administration; an armed citizenry in place of professional forces runs against rule by trained specialists.

rural-life-healthier.rationale: Inferred from the modernist, science-minded outlook of Saint-Simon and Veblen, which treats industry and cities as the sites of progress rather than moralizing rural life.

reunify-divided-nation.rationale: Technocracy is a method of governing and has no stance on national reunification; it depends on the expert assessment of costs and benefits.

educated-out-of-touch.rationale: The ideology rests on trust in expertise and educated competence, so the claim that the educated are out of touch is the populist position it opposes.

cultures-equal-different.rationale: The ideology does not address comparative culture; scientific universalism suggests some ranking by measurable results while its pluralism-averse stance does not settle it.

death-penalty.rationale: Technocrats defer to evidence on the effects of punishment, which varies by case; the ideology does not settle the question.

sex-ed-in-schools.rationale: Technocrats defer to scientific and public-health expertise, which supports evidence-based sex education in schools.

creationism-in-schools.rationale: Technocracy gives authority to scientific expertise, which rejects creationism as unscientific, and Saint-Simon put scientists as the spiritual power.

restrict-pornography.rationale: Not a technocratic concern; the position would turn on expert assessment of harms and adherents are split.

citizenship-by-descent.rationale: Inferred from the universalist, meritocratic bent: citizenship by descent is an ascriptive rule an administrator would see as less rational than residence.

minority-language-support.rationale: Language policy is a matter for expert administration case by case and the ideology has no settled position.

religious-exemptions.rationale: Inferred from the stress on a single common good and uniform expert-set rules, which cut against group-specific exemptions.

encourage-eccentricity.rationale: Not addressed; technocracy is concerned with administration, not with social conformity, and adherents are split.

missingStatements.text: Politics should aim at one common good worked out by reason rather than balancing the competing interests of different groups.
missingStatements.rationale: Anti-pluralism, the pursuit of a single rationally identified general interest instead of mediating between groups, is a defining feature of technocracy in both the reference literature and the scholarship.

notes: Technocracy claims to be value-neutral, so on many social and moral statements it takes no position (0, low confidence); these zeros reflect indifference, not a split. The 1930s Technocracy Inc. strand would answer differently on economics: strongly against markets and money and for central planning (abolish-money-wages +2, central-planning +2, markets-allocate-better -2). Economic answers on the mainstream also split between Keynesian and neoliberal technocrats. The Caramani source was read as its published abstract only.
